claim: Lehman and Yao 1981: each node has a high key and a link pointer to its right twin, so a split leaves two twins joined by the link and the parent pointer is added later; a search whose key lies above the high key follows the link; locks only stop two updaters writing one node.
Lehman and Yao 1981 assume that node reads and writes are atomic and that processes run at comparable speed.
Lehman and Yao 1981 assume that the splitting of a node is an exceptional case.
Levandoski et al. 2013: a Bw-tree page is never updated in place; an update is a delta record prepended to the page by one compare-and-swap on a mapping table.
Levandoski et al. 2013: a thread that sees a partial structure change completes it before its own operation, so no thread waits for a structure change to finish.
Levandoski et al. 2013: on the Xbox workload the Bw-tree reaches 10.4M operations/second against BerkeleyDB's 555K operations/second, a speedup of 18.7x, in memory.
Levandoski et al. 2013: the Bw-tree has an 8.6x speedup over BerkeleyDB on the dedup workload, in memory.
Levandoski et al. 2013: the Bw-tree has a 5.8x speedup over BerkeleyDB on the synthetic workload, in memory.
Levandoski et al. 2013 assume short operations: a split competes with record updates and loses when records are tiny.

Wang et al. 2018 rebuilt the Bw-tree with pre-allocated delta space, decentralised memory reclamation, fast consolidation and search shortcuts, and compared it with SkipList, Masstree, a B+tree with optimistic lock coupling and ART with OLC.
Wang et al. 2018: the Bw-tree under-performs the lock-based indexes by 1.5-4.5x.
Wang et al. 2018: ART is more than 4x faster than the OpenBw-Tree for point lookups, and the OpenBw-Tree is slower than Masstree and the B+Tree, often by a factor of 2x.
Wang et al. 2018: with the lock-free features disabled, the Bw-tree is still 15%-19% slower than the B+tree with OLC.
Wang et al. 2018: the authors' own optimisations speed the Bw-tree up by 27-35%.

Leis et al. 2016: optimistic lock coupling keeps a version counter per node, readers take no lock and validate the version, and a changed node restarts the lookup from the root; ROWEX lets writers lock while readers never block.
Leis et al. 2016: lookup cost in CPU cycles is 418 single-threaded and 2787 at full thread count under lock coupling, and 348 and 418 under optimistic lock coupling.
Leis et al. 2016: lock coupling does not scale well even in lookups although it uses read-write locks; optimistic lock coupling is slightly (around 7%) faster for lookup than ROWEX.
Leis et al. 2019 apply optimistic lock coupling to an in-memory B+tree, as the 2016 paper does for a radix tree.
Leis et al. 2019: with 20 threads, lookup with OLC is 3.9x faster than traditional lock coupling on an in-memory B+tree.
Leis et al. 2019: single-threaded, the three approaches have 'very similar performance' and locking adds 'up to 30% of additional instructions'.
Leis et al. 2019: OLC lookup scales near-linearly up to 20 threads.
Leis et al. 2019 assume in-memory nodes, a version counter per node, and epoch-based or hazard-pointer reclamation of removed nodes.
Mohan and Levine 1992: structure changes in one index are serialised by an X tree latch specific to that index.
Mohan and Levine 1992: a structure modification is performed as a nested top action.
Mohan and Levine 1992 assume the tree latch is held for a very small time, with no I/O inside it.

Srinivasan and Carey 1993 compared B+tree concurrency algorithms (lock coupling with exclusive or SIX locks, optimistic descent, B-link) in a closed queuing simulation of CPUs, disks, a buffer pool and a lock manager.

Srinivasan and Carey 1993, a simulation with no single speed-up ratio in the text: updaters that lock-couple with exclusive locks perform poorly against algorithms that permit more optimistic index descents, and the B-link algorithms give the most concurrency and the best overall performance.

Srinivasan and Carey 1993 (simulation): with 8 disks the pessimistic algorithms level off at around the same maximum throughput, while the optimistic and B-link algorithms gain throughput with increasing MPL.
Srinivasan and Carey 1993 (simulation): with one CPU and one disk the disk is the bottleneck and the only performance difference visible between algorithms is minor.
Srinivasan and Carey 1993 (simulation): on the update-heavy 20/40/40 workload lock coupling is 'even worse'.
Graefe 2010 (survey, no measurements): latches are short and protect a tree's structure among threads; locks are long and protect contents for transactions.
Graefe 2010: in a B-link split the second step, posting the high fence key in the parent, can be made a side effect of any future root-to-leaf traversal and may be delayed beyond a system reboot.
Mohan 1990 (ARIES/KVL): each key value has a lock, each page a short latch, and one tree latch serialises structure changes; an unfinished structure change is flagged on the page (the SM-Bit).
Mohan 1990 (ARIES/KVL): page splits and deletions propagate bottom-up, and SMOs are serialised by acquiring the tree latch in X mode.
Mohan 1990 (ARIES/KVL): a search that meets an unfinished structure change releases its page latches, requests the tree latch in S mode, and restarts its traversal.
Mohan 1990 states that typically no I/O is done while the tree latch is held, so serialising structure changes should not cause a significant reduction in concurrency.
